# pgAudit Open Source PostgreSQL Audit Logging

To limit the number of relations audit logged for `SELECT` and `DML` statements, consider using object audit logging (see Object Auditing). Object audit logging allows selection of the relations to be logged allowing for reduction of the overall log volume. However, when new relations are added they must be explicitly added to object audit logging. A programmatic solution where specified tables are excluded from logging and all others are included may be a good option in this case.
The pgAudit extension must be loaded in shared_preload_libraries. Otherwise, an error will be raised at load time and no audit logging will occur.
Multiple classes can be provided using a comma-separated list and classes can be subtracted by prefacing the class with a `-` sign (see Session Audit Logging).

Specifies the log level that will be used for log entries (see Message Severity Levels for valid levels) but note that `ERROR`, `FATAL`, and `PANIC` are not allowed). This setting is used for regression testing and may also be useful to end users for testing or other purposes.
Session logging is enabled with the pgaudit.log setting.

Object-level audit logging is implemented via the roles system. The pgaudit.role setting defines the role that will be used for audit logging. A relation (`TABLE`, `VIEW`, etc.) will be audit logged when the audit role has permissions for the command executed or inherits the permissions from another role. This allows you to effectively have multiple audit roles even though there is a single master role in any context.
Set pgaudit.role to `auditor` and grant `SELECT` and `DELETE` privileges on the `account` table. Any `SELECT` or `DELETE` statements on the `account` table will now be logged:

Use log_line_prefix to add any other fields that are needed to satisfy your audit log requirements. A typical log line prefix might be `'%m %u %d [%p]: '` which would provide the date/time, user name, database name, and process id for each audit log.
It is not possible to reliably audit superusers with pgAudit. One solution is to restrict access to superuser accounts and use the set_user extension to escalate permissions when required.

The PostgreSQL Audit Extension is based on the 2ndQuadrant pgaudit project authored by Simon Riggs, Abhijit Menon-Sen, and Ian Barwick and submitted as an extension to PostgreSQL core. Additional development has been done by David Steele of Crunchy Data.

Dokku is an open-source version of Heroku.

Dokku uses buildpacks technology to create a Docker image from the code. No Dockerfile needed. Speaking about Python, it requires `requirements.txt`, `Procfile` files to run the things up. Also files `DOKKU_SCALE` and `runtime.txt` are useful to tweak configs to make the deployed app even better. E.g. in `DOKKU_SCALE` you can specify how many app instances should be run behind built-in load balancer.

I assume that you already have Dokku installed on your server. Let's also assume that the address of your server is *<YOURDOMAIN.COM>* (you will need a domain to setup HTTPs for Telegram webhook support). I'd recommend to have at least 2GB RAM and 2 CPU cores.

For Telegram bot API webhook usage you'll need a **https** which can be setup using Letsencrypt Dokku plugin. You will need to attach a domain to your Django app before and specify a email (required by Letsencrypt) - you will receive notifications when certificates would become old. Make sure you achieved a successful deployment first (your app runs at <YOURDOMAIN.COM>, check in browser).

Bindery holds API keys, reaches services on your network and writes to your disks, so it is built and checked with that in mind. Every push and a weekly run go through govulncheck, CodeQL, Semgrep, gitleaks, Hadolint, Checkov, Grype, Syft, a ZAP baseline and OpenSSF Scorecard, with gosec enforced in the blocking lint gate. Release binaries and the container image carry SLSA build provenance, which you can check with `gh attestation verify` (how), and binaries ship with SBOMs. In the app: guards against server side request forgery on outbound URLs, strict response headers, and a distroless non root image with digest pinned bases. The Helm chart adds a read only root filesystem with every capability dropped.
To report a vulnerability, follow **SECURITY.md**. Published advisories are on the Security tab.

Bindery sends one anonymous ping a day to api.getbindery.dev so the maintainer can count active installs and spot widespread breakage, and the reply tells the app when a newer release exists. It carries a random install ID, the version, OS, architecture and deploy method, counts of which features are configured, and the number and fixed text of the most frequent error log lines. Never titles, paths, URLs, usernames, hostnames or IP addresses. Turn it off with `telemetry.enabled: false` in **Settings, Logs**, or `BINDERY_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true` before the first run; the update notice goes with it. Retention and deletion are in **PRIVACY.md**.

Its original purpose was to serve as a demo and test for the KD2 WebDAV library, which we developed for Paheko, our non-profit management solution, but it can also be used as a simple but powerful file sharing server.
Editing a file with Collabora Example of external app integration with oPodSync

If you are looking for an even lighter WebDAV server, try also our other server, PicoDAV. It isn't compatible with NextCloud/ownCloud/OpenCloud clients, but it is a single file that you can drop anywhere in your document root, nothing to install!
* Integrated web file manager (using WebDAV Manager.js):
* Download selected files as a ZIP file
* Support for RFC 3230 to get the MD5 digest hash of a file (to check integrity) on `HEAD` requests (only MD5 is supported so far)
* Support for `Content-MD5` with `PUT` requests, see dCache documentation for details
* Support for some of the Microsoft proprietary properties
* Passes most of the Litmus compliance tests (see below)
* `X-OC-MTime` header to set file modification time (also supported by rclone)
* `OC-Checksum` header to verify file upload integrity

* KDE-based file browsers: Dolphin, Konqueror, Krusader…
* GTK-based file browsers (Thunar, Nautilus, Caja, PCManFM, etc.): they will work, but the GTK implementation is usually slower than KDE
* DAVx⁵ (libre), see the manual for how to set up a WebDAV mount
* rclone works, including bi-directional sync! Pick `NextCloud` as the WebDAV vendor to enable advanced sync features.

* davfs2 is **NOT** recommended: it is very slow, and it is using a local cache, meaning changing a file locally may not be synced to the server for a few minutes, leading to things getting out of sync. If you have to use it, at least disable locks, by setting `use_locks=0` in the config. Other recommended options are `gui_optimize=1` and `delay_upload=0`. See manpage for details.

* csync on Linux (works). This is a library offering two-way sync, it is used by the ownCloud client, but it has a command-line client. Just replace `http` with `owncloud`, and `https` with `ownclouds` in URL, eg. `csync /home/username/sync ownclouds://karadav.example/files/username/`
* Celeste is a Rclone GUI to sync your directories (untested)
* the native webclient (also called 'MiniRedir') **is notoriously bad**. We tested it successfully on Windows 10, but it seems to now be deprecated and scheduled to be removed in Windows 11.
* EasySync (does not allow to sync user-chosen folders sadly)
* WebDAV provider (gives access to WebDAV from other file managers, like DAVx5 does, untested)
* X-Plore (proprietary) has been tested and works, but the app is now full of intrusive video ads, don't use it!
* DrivinCloudOpen is a defunct open-source Android WebDAV client that was easy to use
This depends on the KD2\WebDAV and KD2\WebDAV_NextCloud classes from the KD2FW package, which are packaged in this repository.

* Davros used to be compatible with NextCloud client before version 2.5.0
* FileRun is a proprietary solution compatible with the NextCloud Android app
* webdav: a Go WebDAV server that supports NextCloud thumbnail API
